name: html-to-markdown converters: Turndown (mixmark-io/turndown, formerly domchristie/turndown, JavaScript, formerly 'to-markdown'), MarkItDown (microsoft/markitdown, Python), and Docling (docling-project/docling, IBM Research Zurich, Python)
kind: Three open-source libraries, structurally different in scope: Turndown is a DEDICATED, rule-based HTML-to-Markdown converter (its sole purpose). MarkItDown is a general ANY-FILE-to-Markdown utility (PDF, Office formats, audio, EPUB, email, and HTML) that uses HTML-to-Markdown conversion as one of several converters. Docling is a document-CONVERSION/PARSING toolkit (also multi-format: PDF, DOCX, HTML, EPUB, AsciiDoc, LaTeX, domain XML) oriented specifically toward AI/LLM-pipeline document preparation, with markdown as one of several possible OUTPUT formats (alongside JSON, DocLang, DCLX).
maturity: Turndown: mature, widely adopted (11,000+ GitHub stars), maintained under the mixmark-io org (moved from the original domchristie repo). MarkItDown: actively maintained Microsoft open-source project, has a documented, publicly-tracked security vulnerability (see below) with an active fix discussion, indicating real production use and real security scrutiny. Docling: actively maintained IBM Research project, MIT-licensed, positioned specifically for 'AI-driven document conversion' with an accompanying arXiv paper (2501.17887) describing its architecture -- the most academically-documented of the three.
license: Turndown: MIT (standard for the ecosystem, not independently re-confirmed but consistent with universal JS-library convention). MarkItDown: open-source (Microsoft), exact license not independently re-confirmed in this pass but understood to be permissively licensed given its GitHub-hosted, PyPI-distributed nature. Docling: MIT License, explicitly confirmed ('100% open-source software released under the permissive MIT License'). All three permit use in this project without licensing obstruction.
keeps_and_discards: Turndown KEEPS structural HTML converted rule-by-rule into markdown-equivalent syntax (headings, lists, tables via GFM plugin, task lists, strikethrough) via DOM-tree walking with a customizable RULE system; it DISCARDS or aggressively re-escapes any TEXT CONTENT that happens to resemble markdown syntax (e.g. a heading literally starting with '1. ' gets escaped to '1\. ' so it isn't misread as a list item on re-render) -- a deliberate, if sometimes over-aggressive, escaping policy directly relevant to this project's own roundtrip_safety concerns (item 7). MarkItDown's HTML path KEEPS whatever BeautifulSoup can parse and _CustomMarkdownify (its own subclass of the `markdownify` library's MarkdownConverter) can render, DISCARDING original DOM structure in favor of a text-focused simplification, consistent with its `LLM-pipeline-ingestion` design goal rather than perfect-fidelity round-tripping. Docling KEEPS the richest structural model of the three -- its whole design premise (per its arXiv paper framing) is AI-grade document understanding, meaning it preserves table structure, reading order, and layout-derived hierarchy more aggressively than either Turndown or MarkItDown, at the cost (per the comparison data below) of being ~100x slower than MarkItDown.
structure_preserved: Turndown: preserves markdown-representable structure (headings, lists including nested lists, GFM tables via plugin, blockquotes, code blocks) via its rule-based walker; nested-list and table-syntax handling is explicitly called out in independent commentary as 'important details that separate good converters from mediocre ones,' implying Turndown's own handling of these cases is a real, nontrivial quality axis rather than a solved problem. MarkItDown: comparison data specifically for its PDF path (not HTML) shows near-total STRUCTURAL loss for heading hierarchy -- 'MarkItDown's PDF heading-hierarchy score is about 0.0... doesn't infer heading structure from font size, so every line lands at body level' -- and weak table fidelity (~0.27) versus Docling's TableFormer-backed 0.88; while this specific figure is for PDF input rather than HTML input, it is informative about the LIBRARY's general structural-fidelity philosophy (fast and simple over structurally rich) which likely extends to its HTML path's relative treatment versus Docling's. Docling: the strongest structural preservation of the three, using a dedicated TableFormer model for table structure specifically, and general layout-aware parsing.
interactive_elements: None of the three preserves interactive-control semantics -- all three are text/document-content converters with no notion of button/form/interactive-widget STATE; they convert an interactive control's visible/labeled TEXT content (if any) but not its behavior or state.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not applicable to any of the three -- none has a concept of checked/disabled/expanded/aria state.
layout_awareness: Turndown: NOT layout-aware -- pure DOM-structural rule-matching, no rendering/geometry involved. MarkItDown: NOT layout-aware for its HTML path (BeautifulSoup DOM parsing only); its PDF path's near-zero heading-hierarchy score is DIRECT EVIDENCE of this -- it explicitly does NOT infer structure from visual/font-size cues, a deliberate simplicity-over-fidelity design choice. Docling: THE layout-aware one of the three -- its whole differentiator (per its IBM Research framing and 100x-slower runtime) is using AI-based layout/structure models (TableFormer, general document-layout models) to recover structure that pure DOM/text parsing would miss, which for HTML specifically means it likely still primarily works from DOM/markup rather than rendered pixels (HTML already carries structural markup, unlike a PDF), but its underlying philosophy leans toward heavier structural inference than either of the other two.
javascript_required: None of the three executes JavaScript -- all three operate on already-serialized HTML/markup input (a string or file), not a live rendered page; this means none of them can capture script-rendered/dynamically-injected content on its own, a limitation this project's own live-browser-based sensor does not share and should be noted as a meaningful architectural difference (this project's sensor reads POST-execution DOM state; none of these three libraries do).
evaluation_method: Turndown: no formal benchmark found in available sources; evidence is qualitative (community adoption, star count, documented escaping-rule behavior). MarkItDown vs Docling: a third-party comparison (danilchenko.dev, 2026) benchmarks BOTH on PDF-to-markdown conversion specifically (not HTML-to-markdown), using heading-hierarchy-accuracy and table-fidelity scores as its metrics, plus wall-clock speed comparison -- a REFERENCE-based comparison (implicitly against some ground-truth document structure) though the exact scoring methodology/denominator was not independently confirmed from available sources.
corpus_size_and_origins: Not confirmed for any of the three from available sources -- no page/document-count denominator was found for the MarkItDown-vs-Docling comparison figures (0.0/0.27 vs 0.88), and no benchmark corpus was found for Turndown at all. This is a genuine evidence gap: unlike WCXB or CleanEval (items 1-2), NONE of these three widely-used converter libraries has a publicly known, reproducible, corpus-sized fidelity benchmark specifically for HTML input -- the one comparison figure found is for PDF conversion, a different input modality from this project's own HTML-focused concern.
reported_precision_recall: The only concrete numeric figures found (PDF-conversion-specific, NOT HTML-specific -- flagged clearly): MarkItDown PDF heading-hierarchy score ~0.0, table-fidelity score ~0.27; Docling PDF table-fidelity score 0.88 (TableFormer-backed); MarkItDown reported as running roughly 100x FASTER than Docling. No HTML-specific precision/recall/F1 figures were found for any of the three in this research pass -- a notable and honest gap given this project's own HTML-focused use case.
independent_oracle: The MarkItDown-vs-Docling PDF comparison appears to be an independent third-party benchmark (danilchenko.dev), not vendor-produced by either Microsoft or IBM -- a genuine independence strength for that specific comparison, though its exact ground-truth-construction methodology was not confirmed. No independent oracle was found for Turndown's own fidelity at all, nor for any HTML-specific comparison across the three.
evidence_independence: The PDF comparison's third-party-blog origin gives it reasonable independence from either vendor. MarkItDown's DOCUMENTED SECURITY VULNERABILITY (see failure_modes) is independently reported via a public GitHub issue (microsoft/markitdown#1565), not self-disclosed marketing material -- a genuinely independent, adversarially-motivated finding (a security researcher or user found and reported it), which is a meaningfully strong evidence-independence signal for that specific claim.
page_archetype_coverage: Not addressed by any of the three -- no page-archetype-stratified evaluation was found for any of them, consistent with the general gap noted in corpus_size_and_origins above.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Not addressed by any of the three in available sources.
leaks_outward: MarkItDown's core dependency list (BeautifulSoup, requests, markdownify, magika, charset-normalizer, defusedxml) includes `requests`, meaning at minimum its broader tool (not necessarily its pure-string HTML converter path) is capable of making outbound HTTP requests as part of its normal operation (e.g. fetching a URL to convert) -- a genuine outward-network-access surface this project should be aware of if it ever embeds MarkItDown as a dependency rather than writing its own equivalent conversion logic, since an embedded dependency with its own network capability is a distinct supply-chain/leakage surface from a pure in-process text transform.
mechanism_detectability: Not applicable -- none of these three interacts with a live page/server in a way that could be 'detected'; they are offline string/file transforms.
countermeasures: Not applicable in the privacy-hardening sense for any of the three, though MarkItDown's `defusedxml` dependency IS itself a countermeasure -- specifically for XXE (XML External Entity) attacks in its DOCX-preprocessing path (see failure_modes), demonstrating the project's maintainers are actively aware of and defending against at least one class of document-parsing security risk.
measured_fidelity_cost: The clearest measured cost tradeoff among the three: MarkItDown trades STRUCTURAL FIDELITY for SPEED versus Docling (100x faster, but near-zero heading-hierarchy accuracy and much weaker table fidelity on PDF input) -- an explicit, quantified fast-vs-faithful tradeoff directly analogous in SHAPE (if not domain) to item 5's dynamic-vs-static web-archive-crawling tradeoff. No equivalent measured tradeoff was found for Turndown, which occupies a different niche entirely (pure HTML input, not multi-format document parsing).
gate_state_at_capture: Not applicable -- none of the three is a capture tool; they operate on already-obtained HTML/document content, with no notion of the access conditions under which that content was originally obtained.
determinism: Turndown's rule-based, DOM-tree-walking architecture is deterministic given fixed input and fixed rule configuration (no ML/inference step involved). MarkItDown's HTML path (BeautifulSoup + markdownify subclass) is similarly deterministic for HTML input specifically (its OTHER converters, e.g. audio transcription, are not, but that is outside this item's HTML-focused scope). Docling's use of AI-based structural models (e.g. TableFormer) for RICH structural inference introduces potential NON-determinism or at least model-version-dependence that pure rule-based Turndown/MarkItDown-HTML-path do not share -- an important reliability-axis difference: Docling's added fidelity for complex documents comes with a corresponding loss of the simple determinism guarantee the other two provide.
determinism_across_versions: Not directly addressed by any source, though inferable: Turndown and MarkItDown's HTML-path being pure rule-based code means version-to-version output drift would only occur via explicit rule CHANGES (a normal software-versioning concern, not a model-drift concern); Docling's AI-model-backed structural inference (TableFormer etc.) introduces an ADDITIONAL version-drift axis (a retrained or updated model producing different structural judgments on the same input) that the other two do not have.
reproducibility: High for Turndown and MarkItDown's HTML path (deterministic, rule-based, easily re-run to the same output); Docling's AI-model dependency means reproducibility requires PINNING the specific model version used, not just the library version -- a distinction this project should track if it ever benchmarks or depends on Docling specifically.
failure_modes: The single most concrete, load-bearing finding in this item: MarkItDown has a documented, PUBLICLY-TRACKED, HIGH-SEVERITY XXE (XML External Entity) injection vulnerability in its DOCX pre-processor (GitHub issue microsoft/markitdown#1565), arising from using `xml.etree.ElementTree.fromstring` on UNTRUSTED input without the `defusedxml` protection that the library's OWN dependency list includes but was not (at least as of the issue's filing) consistently applied at that specific code path -- 'any application processing untrusted DOCX files is potentially vulnerable, including web services accepting document uploads, CI/CD pipelines processing documentation, and AI/LLM pipelines using markitdown for document ingestion.' This is a directly transferable, concrete lesson: a library declaring a security-hardening dependency (`defusedxml`) does NOT guarantee that dependency is actually applied at every vulnerable code path -- dependency presence is not evidence of complete mitigation, an important due-diligence lesson for THIS project if it ever adopts any third-party document-parsing library rather than writing its own equivalent logic. Turndown's own most-cited failure mode is over-aggressive escaping (the '1. Hello world' -> '1\. Hello world' example) -- a FALSE-POSITIVE-escaping problem (escaping content that didn't need it) rather than a false-negative (missing an actual injection risk), a different failure CLASS from MarkItDown's XXE issue but still a genuine fidelity/roundtrip concern for item 7's escaping-policy interest.
failure_visibility: MarkItDown's XXE vulnerability is LOUD in the sense that it is publicly filed, tracked, and discussed on GitHub (not silently patched without disclosure) -- a positive transparency signal for the project even though the underlying vulnerability itself was, by definition, a SILENT failure mode for any application unknowingly exposed to it before the report. Turndown's escaping behavior is documented and user-overridable (via `TurndownService.prototype.escape`), a loud, configurable failure-mode-avoidance path rather than a silent one.
scale_limits: The MarkItDown-vs-Docling 100x speed differential IS a scale-limit data point: Docling's richer structural inference imposes a real, order-of-magnitude throughput cost, meaning a large-scale ingest pipeline choosing Docling-equivalent structural richness over MarkItDown/Turndown-equivalent speed is making an explicit, quantified scale-vs-fidelity tradeoff, directly relevant if this project ever needed to choose between a fast-and-simple versus rich-and-slow HTML/document-to-markdown conversion strategy at scale.
delta_cost_model: Not applicable -- none of the three has an incremental-update concept; each is a whole-document, one-shot conversion.
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable -- none of the three has a DOM-element-identity/re-anchoring concept; each produces a flat markdown string output with no persistent mapping back to specific source DOM nodes (a real GAP relative to this project's own architecture, which DOES care about xpath-level provenance -- none of these three libraries would preserve that mapping without significant custom modification).
adversarial_exposure: MarkItDown's XXE vulnerability IS a concrete instance of adversarial exposure (a maliciously crafted DOCX file exploiting the unguarded XML parse path) -- directly relevant evidence that DOCUMENT-PARSING libraries in this exact category (multi-format-to-markdown converters) are a REAL, not hypothetical, attack surface, reinforcing this project's own caution about any embedded third-party parsing dependency. Turndown's escaping behavior (aggressive but documented) is a mitigating factor against MARKDOWN-SYNTAX-level injection (content that could be misread as markdown structure on re-render) but says nothing about the SEPARATE HTML-parsing-input-side attack surface (e.g. malformed/malicious HTML exploiting a parser bug), which was not addressed in available sources for any of the three.
provenance_carrying: None of the three carries per-element provenance (source xpath, capture time) through its conversion -- all three produce a flat markdown string with, at best, whole-document-level metadata (e.g. MarkItDown may retain a source filename/MIME type at the document level), a genuine architectural gap relative to this project's own provenance-carrying design goal (item 8's discussion).
roundtrip_safety: Turndown is the most directly relevant of the three to this field: its escaping-rule design is EXPLICITLY built around the exact roundtrip-safety concern this project cares about -- content that would otherwise be misinterpreted as markdown STRUCTURE on a subsequent render (e.g. a heading starting with '1. ') is deliberately escaped to prevent that misinterpretation, i.e. Turndown's own design already implements a rudimentary form of the escaping-policy discipline item 7 recommends, though its own documentation admits this escaping can be 'quite aggressive,' implying a precision-vs-safety tradeoff (over-escaping legitimate content) rather than a perfectly tuned policy. Neither MarkItDown nor Docling's escaping philosophy was directly confirmed from available sources in this pass.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not directly addressed by any of the three as a design goal, though MarkItDown's stated purpose (AI/LLM pipeline ingestion) implies an IMPLICIT design bias toward producing token-efficient, LLM-consumable output, consistent with its speed-over-fidelity tradeoff versus Docling; Docling's own stated purpose ('AI-driven document conversion', per its arXiv paper title) suggests it explicitly targets DOWNSTREAM AI/LLM consumption as well, but with the OPPOSITE fidelity tradeoff (richer structure at higher token/processing cost) -- meaning the two Microsoft/IBM tools represent genuinely different points on the same LLM-ingestion-oriented design spectrum, both explicitly AI-pipeline-motivated but making opposite fidelity/cost choices.
representation_cost: Not directly measured for HTML-specific conversion by any of the three in available sources; the 100x speed differential (MarkItDown vs Docling) is a COMPUTE-cost figure, not a token/representation-size figure, and no token-count comparison across the three was found.
what_could_be_adopted: Two concrete, specific mechanisms and one explicit non-adoption. ADOPTABLE: (1) Turndown's ESCAPING-RULE PHILOSOPHY (detect content that would be misread as markdown structure on re-render, and escape it) as a direct design input for this project's own markdown-escaping policy discussed in item 7 -- though this project should tune the aggressiveness more carefully than Turndown's own admittedly-aggressive default, since over-escaping ALSO degrades fidelity, just in a less dangerous direction than under-escaping. (2) The GENERAL LESSON from MarkItDown's XXE vulnerability: any third-party parsing dependency this project ever adopts must be independently security-audited at EVERY code path, not assumed safe because a hardening dependency (defusedxml) merely appears in the project's manifest -- dependency presence is not proof of correct application. NOT ADOPTABLE AS A DIRECT DEPENDENCY: none of the three preserves per-element provenance or interactive-element state, both of which are architecturally central to this project -- adopting any of the three as a DROP-IN conversion step would mean losing exactly the properties (xpath-keyed provenance, interactive-element awareness) this project's own capture pipeline is built to preserve; at most, this project could borrow ISOLATED RULES (e.g. Turndown's individual element-conversion rules for headings/lists/tables) while reimplementing the surrounding provenance-carrying architecture itself.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for all three's CONVERSION RULES specifically (converting a `<table>` to markdown table syntax is a syntactic transform, not a region-classification judgment), though Docling's AI-based structural-INFERENCE layer (distinguishing what counts as a meaningful table vs. a layout table, for instance) edges closer to a classifier-like judgment that should be scrutinized if borrowed. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for Turndown and MarkItDown's HTML path (neither reads rendered geometry); Docling's broader philosophy (AI-based structural/layout inference) is the one of the three LEAST aligned with this constraint in spirit, even though its specific HTML-input path likely still works primarily from markup rather than rendered pixels -- worth scrutinizing before borrowing any Docling-specific HTML-handling logic. o_delta: NOT APPLICABLE -- all three are whole-document, one-shot converters with no incremental-update concept; adopting any of their conversion RULES would need to be wrapped in this project's own O(delta)-respecting architecture, not adopted as a whole-pipeline replacement. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS FOR TESTING PURPOSES -- all three are real, runnable, deterministic (or model-pinned) code, suitable for genuine (non-mocked) comparison testing of this project's own markdown-serialization rules against an established reference implementation's output. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT APPLICABLE -- none of the three has any shadow-DOM awareness at all (they operate on already-flattened/serialized HTML strings, meaning shadow DOM content would need to be resolved/flattened BEFORE being handed to any of these three, a preprocessing step this project's own sensor must own regardless of which conversion rules it borrows). OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable in the actuator/implementation layer only, and even then only at the RULE level (individual element-conversion logic, particularly Turndown's escaping approach) rather than as a wholesale drop-in replacement -- none of the three's overall architecture (flat string output, no provenance, no interactive-element model) matches this project's own requirements closely enough to adopt wholesale, and MarkItDown's documented XXE vulnerability is a concrete caution against embedding it (or any similarly-scoped multi-format parser) as a trusted dependency without independent security review.
governance_signal_handling: Not applicable -- none of the three concerns itself with robots.txt/ai.txt/governance signals; they operate on content already obtained by some other means.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not applicable -- none of the three makes any retention or lawful-basis decision; they are pure transformation utilities operating on whatever content they are given, with no independent data-handling policy of their own.
uncertain: No HTML-specific (as opposed to PDF-specific) fidelity benchmark numbers were found for MarkItDown or Docling, despite this being this project's actual use case -- the 0.0/0.27/0.88 figures found are confirmed PDF-conversion numbers only, and their applicability to HTML-input fidelity is inferred/analogous, not directly measured

Whether MarkItDown's XXE vulnerability (GitHub issue #1565) has since been fixed/merged was not confirmed -- the issue was found as an open/tracked report, not confirmed resolved as of this research pass

Turndown's exact GFM-table and nested-list handling QUALITY (as opposed to its mere existence via plugin) was not independently benchmarked in available sources -- only qualitative commentary that this is 'an important detail' was found, not a quantified accuracy figure

Docling's exact HTML-input-specific behavior (as opposed to its PDF-input behavior, which is what the comparison benchmark actually measured) was not independently confirmed -- its HTML support was confirmed to EXIST (InputFormat.HTML, SimplePipeline) but not benchmarked

Exact current MIT/license terms and any recent (post-training-cutoff) security-fix status for all three libraries should be re-verified against their live repositories before this project takes any dependency decision based on this item
